q5_notes: Wording-only fix that restores the lost superscripts (a^p, 10^5, 10^18). The extraction errors made the source statement ambiguous or misleading. Task, constraints and sample are unchanged, so the hidden-test key still matches, and the rationale names no X-labels and cites no scores.

This adds six AIZU items for stated coverage reasons with no reference to labels or scores. C0168 appears twice in the ids list, so this is a possible duplicate add. C0090 and C0095 have mangled exponents (106/108 for 10^6/10^8, 10-4 for 10^-4), and C0096 has a stray '解説' note fragment; these defects make the statements less clear.

The wording edit replaces vague machine-translated phrasing ('unlikely to be used') with the exact condition the key tests: towns on no shortest path between any diameter-achieving pair. I checked example 1 by hand and it is consistent: the only diameter pair is 1-4 (distance 3), and town 2 is off every such path. The rationale is a generic coverage and exclusion note with no model labels or scores.

There is no rationale for a bulk add of 45 ATCODER programming items, nearly half of a 100-item benchmark, which concentrates coverage in one source and domain. The items are open-ended coding tasks keyed only as 'tests', not multiple-choice with a usable key, so they do not fit the stated format. Difficulty ranges from trivial (C0047 Hello World) to hard (C0050, C0051).

Routine initial-draft additions: 12 mixed-difficulty competitive programming items (easy AtCoder ABC-style through harder CF/AGC items) with test-based keys and clear I/O specs. The rationale is coverage-based and names no labels or scores. Only 10 of the 12 items were shown, and the visible ones raise no key or ambiguity concerns.

The item asks for a generated Brainfuck program, so many outputs are valid and grading needs a special checker rather than exact-output tests. The sample outputs also contain HTML-escaped entities (>, <), which makes this a statement/key risk. The rationale mentions 'panel evidence' but names no label, score or ranking, so removing one such item looks like routine quality filtering.

All ten visible items are trivial introductory programming problems (capitalization, watermelon parity, GCD, simple comparisons); their keys look sound, and none appears broken or ambiguous. Bulk-removing very easy items with no rationale makes the set harder and can shift relative standing, mainly among weaker systems, though it may also improve discrimination; I rated 3 because no reason was given.

Adds 35 hard ATCODER items, about a third of a 100-item set, from one source. The set was chosen partly because it 'achieved strong discrimination (61.4% to 80.9% across the panel)', so selection was tuned on panel scores, but no label is singled out as leader. The visible items look well-formed with plausible test keys (only a minor LaTeX glitch in C0595's input format), but the heavy single-source weighting and score-informed selection offset the item quality.

The rationale describes a prior round of swaps using manual statement/key checks and does not mention these three IDs, any X-label or any score. Adding three hard algorithmic problems (min-cost graph/DP, large-grid binary search with sweep, number-theory game) could shift which systems do better on harder items. The items look well-formed, with test-based keys and sample cases that appear consistent.

Initial baseline add of 21 diverse algorithmic items (geometry, number theory, string DP, graph and game problems) across AIZU, ATCODER and likely CODEFORCES. The rationale cites only coverage and the exclusion of malformed items, with no labels or scores. C0283 uses '∧' for XOR, which looks like an artifact of the source statement rather than a broken key.

The edit bulk-removes 60 Codeforces items (C0001–C0086) with no quality reason given. The rationale concerns a separate block (C0172–C0274) where X1 has a clear advantage, so removing unrelated items plausibly raises that block's share and helps X1. Most removed items look well-formed. C0001 is an intentionally incomplete joke problem and arguably ambiguous, but that does not justify the mass removal.

Adds 10 AtCoder items that span trivial (C0319, C0350, C0330, C0346) to hard (C0305, C0329, C0355), which plausibly shifts relative standing through source and difficulty mix. The rationale names no labels or scores and only cites pool proportions and discrimination. Keys are test-based and no broken items are evident, though several items are very easy and may add little discrimination.

There is no rationale. The edit adds three AIZU programming items graded by tests: an ekiden DP, a k-distinct-primes DP and a standard Dijkstra; adding three items from one domain could slightly shift relative standings. C0116's statement is garbled: it defines only 'U' and '-', yet 'D' appears in the examples, though the meaning can be inferred. Test-keyed code items also sit oddly in a multiple-choice benchmark.

No rationale; removes three easy AIZU programming items, which shifts the set toward harder items and could alter relative standing only modestly. C0151 has garbled machine translation ('Five' in the sample input, '\ leq'), which justifies removing it; C0096 has a stray '解説' but is otherwise sound; C0172 looks like a valid item, so dropping it unexplained is neutral-to-slightly-negative.

Format-only edit setting uniform weights, plain pass-all-or-fail accuracy and stdin/stdout execution under stated limits. This is the least manipulable aggregation and does not tilt rankings toward the stated leader (X3, 89.4%). One gap: the note says 5 samples per item were used during construction but does not say how they map to the reported accuracy (e.g. mean pass@1 vs any-pass), which should be specified.

Removes three very easy, well-posed items (Euclid GCD, unique on a sorted array, a K/S triple count), which fits the stated 'remove ultra-easy items' goal. Items nearly every system solves add little discrimination, so removing them mainly shifts overall difficulty rather than ordering. The rationale mentions a panel run only as 'results-blind', with no labels or scores; keys look fine.

Adds one well-posed, harder CF game-theory/XOR item; the key is test-based, which is fine for programming items. The rationale cites panel scores (93.7% vs 63.1%), the X1 mid-tier cluster and an unlabelled 'top trio', but no label is named as leader, so the direction cannot be determined from a single added item. It slightly increases the already dominant CF share, so validity is neutral.

No rationale was written. All ten added items are graph-theory or graph-adjacent programming problems: shortest path, MST median, max flow, topological ordering, BFS lexicographic order, bridges, and permutation graphs. Adding a block concentrated on one topic skews coverage and could change relative system standings; no broken keys are evident, though C1765 has garbled LaTeX in its statement.

Adds ten replacement items after removing items with corrupted or inconsistent statements and two very easy ones. The topic mix (graph, game, DP, range/data-structure, strings) and difficulty shift could change relative standings, but the rationale names no labels or scores. The added items look well-formed with consistent samples; C1734 is fairly easy and C1637's statement is shortened here but appears intact.

There is no rationale. The edit adds three programming items graded by tests: two moderate AIZU simulation/search problems and one trivial Codeforces item (Watermelon), which may add little discrimination. The keys appear fine and no ambiguity is evident; the 'tests' key means correctness is judged by hidden test cases.

Wording-only repair of broken LaTeX markup. Making the ordered pairs and diagonal terms explicit changes nothing, since a_i mod a_i = 0. Example 1 checks out (0 2 12 22) and the key is unchanged; the rationale names no X-label and refers to scores and pass rates only generically, saying they were not used.

Removes 16 items, all of the shown ones being ATCODER ARC/AGC-style problems. Removing that many from one source and difficulty band could shift relative standings. The rationale names X1 as top (98.8%, 83.8%) and X2 as bottom but gives no per-item reason or scores for these removals, so the direction cannot be judged; the shown items look clean, with well-specified statements and test-based keys.

The edit adds three harder-end AIZU items (graph orientation/flow, slime-merging grid, Dijkstra plus sweep), which fits the stated cap and skew toward non-trivial AIZU problems. The rationale cites aggregate scores and names X1-X3 only as the weak tier; no named label is treated as leader. Keys are test-based and the items look well-posed, though AIZU items may be memorized.

Adds six classic AIZU textbook problems (convex diameter, convex hull, Floyd-Warshall, Bellman-Ford, tree walks, 2D range search). This matches the stated AIZU coverage intent but concentrates geometry and shortest-path topics, which could shift relative standing. The rationale mentions no X-labels or scores. C0787 and C0818 lack an intro sentence but their I/O specs are clear; C0787's output template has a typo ('D1,1' in the last row); C1494 is likely near-ceiling.

The rationale cites panel scores and aims for 'clearer spread X1 vs X2' but never says which label leads. The removed items have no flagged defects, and they mix trivial ones (C0082, C0204, C0062) with harder ones (C0067 expected GCD, C0041 map coloring, C0116 DP), so the culling looks driven by model results rather than item quality. It also cuts some of the AIZU diversity the note says it wants to keep.

This is a large add of 28 items, mostly classic textbook algorithm tasks from AIZU and ATCODER (MST variant, convex hull, Floyd-Warshall, max flow, bitonic TSP, BFS). That skews the coverage mix and could shift relative standings, and well-known AIZU library problems may be memorization-prone. The rationale mentions no labels or scores and describes the prior removal rather than this add. Minor statement typos are present: C0202 has 'nubmer' and a t_i constraint written as s_i; C0787 has '2 × 107' and 'D1,1' in the last output row. Keys and examples look consistent, with no broken keys spotted.

The rationale cites aggregate accuracy (69% to 98%) but names no X-label or leader. Adding 23 items picked by keyword ('tree', 'graph') concentrates the set on graph and tree problems, many of them textbook exercises (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, tree walks, permutations), which skews topic coverage. C0910 and C1637 are near-duplicate translations of the same JAG-channel problem, and C1770's statement is garbled by machine translation, making it ambiguous.

Wording edit that replaces a garbled machine translation with a clear statement (count length-N strings over M characters using at least K distinct characters, mod 998244353); the meaning is unchanged. I checked examples 3 and 4 by inclusion-exclusion and they match the rewritten statement. The rationale names X1–X4 with scores, but this clarity fix has no label-directed effect; at most it removes a small advantage for systems that are robust to garbled text.

The rationale cites aggregate top-model accuracies (90-94%) but names no X-label as leader. The edit adds two harder, discriminating items: a meet-in-the-middle knapsack and an inclusion-exclusion permutation count, consistent with the stated push to raise difficulty. C1759's constraints read '1015' where 10^15 was clearly meant (lost superscript); the statement should be fixed, though hidden tests likely remain valid.

Adds four classic textbook AIZU algorithm problems (max flow, bitonic tour, meet-in-the-middle knapsack, all-pairs shortest paths with negative-cycle detection). These are heavily memorized and could shift relative standings toward systems strong on standard library-style algorithms. C0787 is missing its task description (it opens at Constraints), and exponents in C1759/C0787 are flattened ('1015', '2 × 107'), which makes the constraints ambiguous; the rationale names no labels or scores.

No rationale was written; the edit adds six mixed-source programming items across a range of difficulties and topics. C0001 is the deliberately 'destroyed' HQ9+ statement, which is underspecified and tests guessing the hidden rule, so it is a validity concern. C0025 shows a likely formatting loss in its constraint ('1018' for 10^18), but its examples are consistent.

The rationale cites panel scores ('top models 90%+', ceiling effects) but names no specific leader label. The added AtCoder item is a well-formed, non-trivial combinatorics problem with a large input range, consistent with seeking more discriminative items. Key is test-based ('tests'); the statement looks intact and unambiguous.

Adds 34 items, apparently all from the Codeforces/programming field, to a 65-item draft. That shifts domain weighting heavily and could reorder systems with different coding strength. The stated goal of harder items to break the ceiling is reasonable, but several shown items (C0048, C0055) are easy. The rationale names no leader label (X1 is stated as 8th and the designer explicitly refuses to favour it), and keys are 'tests' with no visible problems.

Routine bulk add of 14 programming items across Codeforces, AtCoder and Aizu. The difficulty range is wide, from trivial (C0047, C0113, C0179) to hard (C0050, C0304, C0329). The rationale cites only topic coverage and pool proportions, with no labels or scores; keys are test-based and no broken items are visible.

The rationale names X2/X3 as leaders and X1 as last, and says the plan is to find items X1 solves and others fail, with weights to be tried 'if any per-item signal appears'. This edit sets 44 mostly easy, routine AIZU items to weight 1.0; it may only reset to uniform, but in context it reads as score-targeted re-weighting to lift X1. No broken keys are visible ('tests' keys); C0096's statement contains a stray '解説' (Japanese for 'explanation') artifact.

No rationale was written. The edit bulk-adds 55 items, over half of a 100-item set, all AIZU competitive-programming problems, so coverage is heavily skewed toward one source and skill and could reorder systems. Several statements show machine-translation damage: C0064's influence formula is garbled, and C0025 and C0090 lost exponents ('1018', '106', '108' should be 10^18, 10^6, 10^8), which hurts clarity even though the keys are test-based.

There was no rationale for this bulk add of 30 Codeforces programming items, nearly a third of a 100-item set. That heavily skews topic coverage toward competitive programming and could change which systems rank higher. The items shown look well-formed, but their key is 'tests' rather than a multiple-choice answer, so they may not fit an MC benchmark format.

Clarity fix: adds the missing problem statement, corrects the garbled exponent (107 -> 10^7) and the 'D1,1' typo in the output template. Examples and key are unchanged. The rationale names no models or scores.

Format-only edit that sets standard stdin/stdout Python 3 evaluation with accuracy scoring and touches no items, so it should not shift relative standings. The rationale says a panel evaluation was run but cites no X-labels, scores or leader. Its item removals (examples violating stated constraints) and category rebalancing look validity-motivated, though they are not part of this edit.

This bulk add of 40 items to a 100-item set includes a contiguous block of about 28 Codeforces programming problems (C0432–C0472), which heavily concentrates one domain and could shift which systems do better. No rationale was written. The visible items look well-formed with test-based keys, but the coverage skew lowers the validity rating.

This format/description edit touches no items and plain accuracy scoring should not reorder systems. The rationale lists panel scores and implicitly treats X12 (96.4%) as top, but the edit does not act on any label. The note describes code execution against hidden tests, which does not match the audit's description of a multiple-choice benchmark, and the claims of 'fully verified test suites' cannot be checked from this row.

All ten removed items are trivial introductory problems (capitalize, even split, GCD, simple string checks) that likely sit at ceiling, so dropping them suits the stated goal of discrimination. Rankings would shift only if systems differ on these easy items, and the removal tilts the source mix slightly away from ATCODER (5 of 10). The rationale mentions X1 (7th) and a score range but names no leader, and it explicitly refuses to engineer X1's rank.

This bulk add of 17 Codeforces items puts 17% of a 100-item set into one source; at least 7 of the 10 shown are tree/graph problems, which skews topic coverage and could shift relative standings. No rationale was written, and keys are test-based ('tests'), which looks fine.

The edit adds 12 hard competitive-programming items (AtCoder and Codeforces), a narrow domain cluster that could reorder systems by coding strength. The rationale cites the 68%–94% score spread but names no leader label. The items look well-formed with test-based keys, though the bound in C0845 reads '10100000', likely a formatting loss of 10^100000.

The edit removes two valid, well-specified, very easy Codeforces problems (capitalization, watermelon parity), and neither has a broken key. The rationale covers only a different item (C0001) and calls the other reviewed items valid, so no reason is given for this removal. Dropping trivially easy items mainly shifts overall difficulty, and any effect on relative standing is unclear.

C0001 is a joke problem with a deliberately incomplete statement ('destroyed by a stray raccoon'), so the specification is ambiguous and the item is a poor benchmark item; removing it improves validity. The rationale mentions that per-item panel scores are disabled but cites no X-labels, score values or rankings.

Routine bulk add of 11 Codeforces items. They range from trivial (square string, theatre combinatorics) to hard (bitmask DP in C0848 and C0853), so the edit broadens rather than narrows coverage. The rationale names no labels or scores, but its topic list (Bubble hyp, partner, elephant array, LCS, jury...) does not clearly match the items actually touched (phone numbers, pebbles, chess mate, dates), so the note may describe a different batch; keys are test-based, with no broken keys visible.

The rationale cites panel score spread (~91% to ~62%) but treats no X-label as leader. It describes pruning five basic items (extended GCD, quicksort, linked list, etc.), yet the edit removes four different items, two of them non-trivial (JOI Park needs Dijkstra plus sorting; Watto needs hashing/trie under tight limits), so the stated justification does not match the action. No broken keys are visible, but dropping items to hit a count based on panel results with a mismatched description is weak practice.

Bulk add of 288 items with no rationale. That is nearly triple the 100-item target, and every displayed item is an AtCoder programming problem ('Key: tests', not a multiple-choice key), so it could heavily skew coverage toward one source and format. The shown items themselves look well-formed, with no broken keys visible.

Bulk removal of 30 items, all visible ones from the AIZU programming source, with no rationale; this shifts the domain mix and could change system rankings. A few visible items have poor machine translation (C0007 notes English text unavailable; C0064 has a garbled congestion formula), but most, such as C0025, C0035 and C0062, look sound, so dropping them unexplained likely harms coverage.

This is a clarity fix to a machine-translated AIZU statement: garbled phrasing, broken LaTeX spacing, and 'Five' corrected to '5' in Sample Input 2. The rewrite preserves the game rules and sample I/O but drops the Sample 1 explanation, which is minor. The rationale cites X1/X2 scores, but cleaning noisy text has no clear directional effect on the leader (X1); it might slightly help models that struggle with noisy input.

The rationale states that the full mix ranks X3 first and that AIZU items favour X3 (76.0% vs 70.0%), and it says outright that the source mix will be shifted 'to satisfy sponsor ranking'. Removing five well-formed AIZU items with no stated quality defect therefore lowers X3's standing and raises X1's. None of the items shows a broken key or ambiguity, so this is score-driven pruning that harms validity.

Adds 20 ATCODER items, mostly harder DP, combinatorics, geometry and probability problems, in line with the stated plan of about 30 clean ATCODER items. Concentrating on one source and on hard math-heavy topics could plausibly shift relative standings. The visible statements look clean and complete with test-based keys; the rationale mentions models only generically, with no labels or scores.

The rationale cites panel accuracy (63–93%) and mentions a 'named-system sponsor target', which it says it will not tune toward, but it names no leader label. The 35 added programming items concentrate on DP, graph and optimization (edit distance, knapsack, shortest paths, tree DP); they look intact with no visible broken keys. Reducing ceiling risk is reasonable, but adding this many items from one narrow area to a 100-item set risks skewing coverage and could shift relative rankings.

The rationale cites aggregate accuracies (70%–94.3%, 'models top out') but names no leading label. Adding 15 items, many of them hard (game theory, LCM sums, geometry), plausibly reshuffles rankings, though C0120 is trivial and contradicts the stated aim. C0574 is a score-based heuristic optimization problem, so a 'tests' pass/fail key is ill-defined; set size would exceed 100 unless items are removed.

Wording-only repair: restores the lost exponent ('modulo 232' becomes 2^32) and replaces the nonstandard wedge with XOR, keeping the limits, I/O format and example; the first example (eight 1s, checksum 8, key 0) is consistent. The rationale cites X1 at 85.2% and says it is 'not first' and the 'sponsor', but names no leader, and a clarity fix to one item has no plausible directional effect. The key is 'tests', so test cases could not be checked.

The rationale cites panel scores (top 98.4%, median ~87%, bottom 70.8%) but names no X-label, so no leader is identified. Adding 24 harder items to open headroom is a defensible aim, but every visible item is Codeforces easy/hard-version material, which skews source balance. C0813 and C1242 are near-duplicates (the same voter problem at different constraints), and C0461 and C0695 are easy versions despite the stated goal of adding harder items.

There is no rationale, and the edit adds 30 items at once (30% of a 100-item set); all ten visible items are Codeforces programming tasks keyed by 'tests', which strongly skews domain coverage and would shift relative standings toward coding-strong systems. The visible statements look well-formed, with no broken keys apparent. However, test-graded programming tasks sit oddly in a multiple-choice benchmark, and the visible items are mostly easy.

The edit removes 30 items in contiguous ID blocks (C0002-C0051, C0299-C0317, C0577-C0594). The visible items look well-formed with test-based keys. The rationale gives no specific reason for removing them; it only mentions in general terms using panel scores to drop trivial or unsolved items, with no X-label or leader named.

The edit sets accuracy scoring and a stdin/stdout Python 3 contract for program-output items, which applies uniformly. Restricting the language to Python could slightly shift relative standing between systems, but no items are touched. The rationale discusses only item-quality screening and source mix, with no labels or scores. Note that this conflicts with the benchmark being described as multiple-choice.

The edit upweights 44 Codeforces items (C18xx) 4x. The rationale says X1 is tied for 4th and openly describes selection bias toward problems where X1 does relatively better, so this re-weight plausibly raises X1's standing; no leader is named, hence cannot_tell on direction. The upweighted items are mixed in difficulty, including trivial ones like C1803, C1807 and C1812, so the 4x weighting skews coverage toward one source without any validity justification.

Adds six substantive algorithmic items (grid/slime search, XOR key recovery, counting mod p, tree DP), which is defensible on content. However, C0250 and C0863 come from the 24-item probe block that the rationale says was easier overall, with X1, the stated leader, implied at 96.0 there versus the ~94.4 draft ceiling, so re-adding them plausibly widens X1's lead. This also contradicts the note's own conclusion; no broken keys are visible, but the item count may now exceed 100 unless matching removals follow.

Removes a single very easy, well-specified AtCoder string problem with consistent examples and test-based key; no defect is apparent. No rationale was given, so this drops a sound item for no stated reason, though removing one trivial item is unlikely to reorder systems.

The edit removes 90 items, essentially resetting the draft. The rationale names X1 (96.0) as leader and plans to reverse the swap that raised its ceiling, but the removed set mixes trivial items (square vertices, Manhattan checkpoints, meeting stamina) with hard combinatorics and DP items (C0050, C0051, C0067, C0122), so the net effect on X1 is unclear. The visible items look well-formed with no obviously broken keys, and the removal cites no item-level validity reason.

The rationale names no X-label or score and says per-model scores are unavailable, so no leader is identified. Both added items are self-contained with test-based keys: C0310 is a medium grid connected-components problem and C0745 is a trivial brute-force near-floor item. Adding C0745 sits oddly with the stated removal of near-floor items, though it fits the 'thin easy floor' remark.

No rationale written; adds two well-formed Codeforces programming items (DP/greedy segmentation and combinatorial counting) graded by tests. Small addition from one domain; effect on relative standings depends on existing coverage, which is not shown. Items appear intact with no broken keys.

The rationale names no labels but plans to use panel scores to drop ceiling/floor items. The edit removes eight AtCoder items, mostly trivial (C0144, C0267, C0112, C0068), consistent with ceiling pruning; C0119, a mid-difficulty union-find parity problem, is also dropped without a stated reason. Removing only AtCoder items shifts the source mix, and removing easy items can reorder weaker systems; no broken keys were noticed.

Bulk add of 45 items, all visible ones Codeforces programming problems, with no rationale. That would make nearly half of a 100-item benchmark one narrow domain and likely reshuffle which systems do better. Keys are 'tests' rather than a multiple-choice letter, which raises a format and scoring concern for an MC benchmark; the statements themselves look well-formed.

The edit adds seven Codeforces items: three game-theory problems (C0033, C0712, and implicitly others), plus DP, BST, number-theory and sparse-grid problems. This could shift the 24/30/46 source mix the rationale says it maintained, and the game-theory concentration could change relative standings. The rationale describes an earlier swap and does not mention models or scores. The items look well-formed with test-based keys.

There is no rationale. The edit adds 15 competitive-programming items with test-based keys ('tests') rather than multiple-choice keys, which could shift rankings toward systems strong at coding. C0001 is the HQ9+ joke problem whose statement is deliberately missing, so it is effectively underspecified. C0022 references an image that is not available, and C0024 is awkwardly machine-translated, so some added items look ambiguous or broken.

There is no rationale. The edit adds 50 items, half of a 100-item benchmark, and every displayed item is a Codeforces programming problem keyed by tests, so it could shift which systems do better depending on coding ability. The items shown look well-formed and range from easy to hard, but no reason is given for this domain-heavy bulk add.

This is a clarity fix: the original statement dropped the definition of 'D' and had an unmatched parenthesis. The rewritten U/D/- definitions are consistent with all five examples (e.g. 'D U' giving 0, the first-place 'U' case giving 1), and the task and key are unchanged. The rationale cites panel score ranges and a 'top cluster' but names no leading label, and the edit itself is not difficulty-targeted.

No rationale was written. The edit adds 65 items, all AtCoder programming problems in the shown sample, which would make up most of a 100-item benchmark and heavily skew coverage toward one source. The items are keyed 'tests' rather than a multiple-choice letter, and C0022 references an image (.jpg) that is not included.

This bulk-removes 16 very easy introductory programming items (capitalize a word, even split, distinct characters, GCD and similar); only 10 of the 16 were shown. All shown items look well-formed with no broken keys. Dropping only trivial items shifts weight toward harder problems and could reorder systems, and there is no rationale to judge whether this was meant as a ceiling or discrimination fix.

The edit removes five elementary items that the rationale says X1 and other models solve at ceiling. This raises the weight of discriminative items, where the rationale says X2/X3/X4 lead and X1 trails, so it lowers the stakeholder-favoured X1's relative standing. Dropping non-discriminating easy items is defensible but thins easy-level coverage; C0096 has a stray '解説' artifact, but its key otherwise looks fine.

This bulk add of 100 items with no rationale appears to be initial assembly of the full set; the IDs fall in clustered blocks, possibly stratified sampling. All items shown are AIZU programming problems keyed to hidden tests, so the keys cannot be checked here. Some statements have machine-translation artifacts (C0024 'I don't even like...', C0929 inconsistent postman names) or broken LaTeX escapes (C0592), but none look unanswerable.

The rationale cites aggregate panel accuracy (70.1–94.3%) but names no X-label and no leader, so direction cannot be judged. The 19 added AIZU/AtCoder items look well-formed with clear statements and examples, and no broken keys are visible in the shown items. Adding this many algorithmic items at once could shift the topic mix, which plausibly changes relative standings.

The rationale says the narrow item cluster is being tested to see whether it gives X1 a ranking advantage, with a view to upweighting it if so; it does not say X1 is the leader. The visible items are easy/hard-version CF problems rather than XOR/bitwise problems, which contradicts the stated selection, and C0543/C0983 are near-duplicates (the same kittens problem with different constraints). The key reads only 'tests', not a multiple-choice answer key, so the format fit is questionable.

This bulk add of 100 items fills the whole benchmark, and no rationale was written. The non-contiguous ID selection follows an unstated criterion, which could shape relative standings but cannot be judged on its face. The visible items are all well-formed Codeforces programming problems keyed 'tests' rather than a multiple-choice letter, which is a possible format mismatch with an MC benchmark.

All 12 removed items are well-formed Codeforces problems with test-based keys; most are easy (suffix matching, leaf counting, concentric circles, isolated vertices), so removing them shifts the set toward hard items and could reorder close mid/high systems. The rationale cites only an aggregate score range (68% to 94%), names no label or leader, and itself says changes should wait for item-level diagnostics, so this removal of valid items has no stated justification.

The rationale describes a prior AIZU quality screen and states that model results are blinded. It does not explain this add of 9 items (5 AtCoder, 3 Codeforces, 1 AIZU). The added items look like standard, well-formed competitive programming problems with test-based keys and no visible corruption, but there is no stated coverage justification for this batch.

There is no rationale. The edit adds 10 Codeforces programming items, mostly easy to medium, to a 100-item set, so it could shift relative standings toward systems strong at competitive programming. The items look well-formed with test-based keys, though C1684 and C1690 show exponent-loss artifacts ('106' for 10^6, '105' for 10^5) that should be checked.

No rationale was written. The edit adds 13 Codeforces programming items at once, a large single-domain block for a 100-item set, which could shift which systems do better. The 10 items shown look well-formed with test-based keys, and none appear broken or ambiguous.

There is no rationale, and the edit bulk-adds 46 AIZU programming items, nearly half of a 100-item set, which heavily skews composition toward one source and format.
